lesson.title: Routing Algorithms: The Rulebook for Finding a Good Path
lesson.summary: A routing algorithm is the formal procedure routers use to compute least cost paths through the network, and routing algorithms fall into two broad families based on how much of the network each router is allowed to know.
lesson.body:
Once you accept that a router's job is to figure out the best next hop toward every destination, a natural question follows: best according to what, and computed how. That is the job of a routing algorithm. It is useful to think of a network as a graph: routers are nodes, the links between them are edges, and each edge has a cost, which might represent distance, delay, bandwidth, or simply a number an administrator assigned by hand. A routing algorithm's job is to take that graph and compute, for each router, the least cost path to every other point in the network.

Routing algorithms generally fall into one of two families, distinguished by how much of the graph each router is allowed to see. In a global, or link state, approach, every router eventually learns the complete map, every node and every edge cost, and independently computes shortest paths over the whole thing. In a decentralized, or distance vector, approach, no router ever sees the full picture, each one knows only the cost to its immediate neighbors and gradually improves its estimate of distances to farther destinations by comparing notes with those neighbors, round after round, until the whole network's estimates settle down. The next several chapters focus on this second family in depth.

Neither approach is universally better, each makes different tradeoffs between the amount of information routers must store and exchange, how quickly the network reacts to changes, and how well the approach scales to very large networks. What both families share is the same underlying goal: turn a map of nodes, edges, and costs into a working set of routing table entries, and do it in a way that keeps working as the network's topology shifts underneath it.
